record.title: Authors report frequent context compaction preserves performance across tested long-horizon and long-input tasks
record.summary: In arXiv:2611.05306v1, the authors evaluate context compaction and selective input reading on six long-horizon and seven long-input benchmark families. For end-of-conversation compaction, they report broadly near-baseline accuracy across tested thresholds for Claude Opus 4.5 and GPT 5.6 Sol, alongside estimated optimized retail-cost reductions; the estimates are not observed invoice savings. In a single-action-compaction condition, median live context is 7–9K tokens and maximum context 15–37K, while GPT 5.6 Sol falls 2.0 and 3.3 percentage points below its baselines on two coding benchmarks. These are author-reported results from the tested benchmarks and models; independent reproduction and universal transfer are not established.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: arXiv posted version 1 of “You don’t need long context” on 3 November 2026; the paper evaluates context compaction and selective input reading on long-horizon and long-input tasks.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report that end-of-conversation compaction across six long-horizon benchmarks broadly preserves performance for Claude Opus 4.5 and GPT 5.6 Sol: no more than 5 of 22 context-threshold configurations per model lose over 2 percentage points relative to their full-history baselines.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: For the tested long-horizon configurations, the authors estimate optimized retail serving-cost reductions of 2.2×–8.8× for Claude Opus 4.5 and 2.4×–5.0× for GPT 5.6 Sol; these are estimates derived from throughput and pricing assumptions, not observed invoice savings.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Across seven long-input benchmark families, authors report that selective input reading with compaction as fallback generally matches or improves full-input baseline accuracy while keeping live context shorter; estimated cost reductions vary widely by task and model.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: In single-action compaction experiments on SWE-bench Verified and Terminal-Bench 2.1, the authors report median peak context of 7–9K tokens and maxima of 15–37K, versus baseline maxima of 130–200K; GPT 5.6 Sol scores 82.4% and 84.3%, respectively, 2.0 and 3.3 points below its mini-agent baselines.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: The paper does not establish that short context is sufficient for every task, that compaction never loses task-relevant history, or that estimated savings transfer to other models, workloads, serving systems or realized costs; no independent reproduction was inspected.

evidence_gaps.description: The benchmark results and serving measurements have not been independently reproduced in this activation; paper artifacts and harnesses require a separate audit.

Optimized retail-cost results are estimated from serving-throughput and pricing assumptions rather than measured customer bills; transfer to other hardware, utilization, model/API prices and workload mixes is unknown.
The evaluation covers named benchmark suites and two closed-weight models in the main task study; it does not establish sufficiency of short context for all long-horizon or long-input task classes.

brief.importance_rationale: If the reported task accuracy and serving-cost trade-offs generalize, short-context state management could materially change context-window, agent-harness and inference-serving design choices. The score reflects that consequence in the tested regime, not the truth or universal transferability of this author-reported study.
limitations: All task and throughput outcomes are reported by the paper authors; no independent reproduction was inspected.

The main long-horizon task study uses Claude Opus 4.5 and GPT 5.6 Sol and six benchmark suites. The reported preservation is near-baseline over tested thresholds, not proof that every task tolerates lossy compaction.
The paper explicitly notes tasks can require details that compaction discards; it gives a coin-toss-history example where eventual loss is guaranteed under a fixed compacted state.
Retail-cost benefits are estimated from throughput and pricing assumptions and are not measured invoice savings or general cost multipliers.
Single-action-compaction results are mixed by model: GPT 5.6 Sol falls 2.0 and 3.3 percentage points below its mini-agent baselines on SWE-bench Verified and Terminal-Bench 2.1.

For end-of-conversation compaction, they report broadly near-baseline accuracy across tested thresholds for Claude Opus 4.5 and GPT 5.6 Sol, alongside estimated optimized retail-cost reductions; the estimates are not observed invoice savings. In a single-action-compaction condition, median live context is 7–9K tokens and maximum context 15–37K, while GPT 5.6 Sol falls 2.0 and 3.3 percentage points below its baselines on two coding benchmarks. These are author-reported results from the tested benchmarks and models; independent reproduction and universal transfer are not established.

technical.claimed_result: The authors report that frequent end-of-conversation compaction broadly preserves accuracy on six long-horizon benchmarks; for either tested model, no more than 5 of 22 tested threshold configurations lose more than 2 percentage points relative to full-history baselines. Seven long-input benchmark families generally match or improve on full-input baselines with selective reading and compaction fallback. Single-action compaction keeps median context at 7–9K and maximum at 15–37K; GPT 5.6 Sol records 82.4% on SWE-bench Verified and 84.3% on Terminal-Bench 2.1, 2.0 and 3.3 points below its mini-agent baselines.
technical.compute_or_cost: The paper estimates optimized retail costs using measured throughput converted with stated serving-price assumptions. It reports long-horizon estimated reductions of 2.2×–8.8× for Claude Opus 4.5 and 2.4×–5.0× for GPT 5.6 Sol; long-input estimates vary substantially by benchmark and configuration. These are estimates, not realized invoice costs.
technical.demonstrated_result: The authors published a 31-page technical report with benchmark, model, harness, compaction and serving-measurement methods plus detailed appendices. Quantitative task and systems outcomes remain paper-reported and were not independently reproduced in this activation.
technical.implementation_status: The experiments use end-of-conversation compaction, selective filesystem reading for long inputs, and a one-action-per-context variant. Semantic State Space Models (SSSMs) are proposed as a future model concept, not presented as a trained and validated architecture in this paper.
technical.mechanism: End-of-conversation compaction summarizes accumulated agent history when context reaches a threshold; selective reading uses tools to retrieve portions of long inputs; single-action compaction carries a short semantic state between actions. The paper argues that these mechanisms can reduce live context while retaining task-relevant state in the evaluated settings.
technical.regime: Main task evaluations use Claude Opus 4.5 and GPT 5.6 Sol across six long-horizon and seven long-input benchmark families, with multiple total-context/compaction thresholds. Open-weight throughput measurements use GLM 5.2, Kimi K2.6 and Qwen 3 Coder Next on H100-class serving; local decoding measurements use models on an NVIDIA DGX Spark. Cost results depend on the paper’s workload, price and throughput assumptions.
technical.reproducibility: The full arXiv HTML specifies benchmark suites, model choices, harnesses, task thresholds and appendices with detailed results. No independent execution or reproduction was inspected in this activation; artifact availability and exact replication of all runs remain open.
technical.strongest_baseline: The main comparisons use the same model and benchmark harness under full-history/full-input baselines versus compaction or selective-reading variants. The study includes two closed-weight model families for its primary agent-task evaluations, but is not an exhaustive comparison across models or task classes.

brief.title: Authors report frequent context compaction preserves performance across tested long-horizon and long-input tasks
brief.why_it_matters: Long contexts can increase decode cost and make agent state expensive to serve. If the paper’s results generalize, explicit state compaction and selective retrieval could alter agent-harness and inference-system choices. The evidence is bounded to named tasks, models and settings; some tasks lose accuracy, cost reductions are estimated, and independent reproduction is not established.
